One imagines that, knowing the whole thing is a birthday prank, one would not be driven to suicide (the actor, Michael Douglas, was not driven to suicide in the making of the film). Analogously, in brain retraining one is told the joke before one even begins the work, and thereafter one is told the joke over and over. This actually helps a lot in my experience.

You can observe your crazy thoughts and not identify with them. The sense I get from Buddhist meditation is that you don't try to correct those thoughts either! So you still kind of stay stuck in that frame, because all of the thoughts that your brain generates are from within that frame, of "I have a physical illness". I think brain retraining adds what Dan Buglio calls "clarity", as in clarity about what is causing the symptoms (different from what Shinzen Young calls "clarity", by which he means sensory clarity), i.e. a new frame, a new explanation for the symptoms, a new generator of thoughts for your brain. I was struck by what Romeo Stevens said in his First Five Years of Practice interview. At one point, around the 55:18 mark, he says that in response to the COVID pandemic he could "watch the mammal get stressed" (which I interpret as him saying that he could observe that his body and lower-level parts of the mind were doing mammalian things like wanting safety and comfort) and his sleep wasn't as good, but that he didn't suffer that much from it. Imagine though someone who had no experience with meditation but who at the start of the pandemic believed that COVID either was not a real virus or that it was no worse than the flu. Such a person would have even less stress than Romeo; there just wouldn't be anything to be stressed about! Note that this is orthogonal to the question of whether COVID really is a threat. The point is simply that thoughts and emotions emerge out of background beliefs one has about the world. If a threat is real, then it's better to believe that and to try to stay calm anyway, whereas if a threat is fake, then it's obviously better not believe the threat and then not have any stress. Brain retraining says that your symptoms are kind of fake, as in, the symptoms themselves are very much real but the cause of the symptoms is not what you think it is, and this allows you to have better, less stress-inducing thoughts. So that is the first big difference between brain retraining and meditation/therapy.

The second difference is that brain retraining, at least the way I prefer to do it, does not happen inside designated blocks of time, but rather happens continuously as one is living life. Basically any practice can be done in a "formal practice" way or a "life practice" way. For example, one may lift weights at the gym, which is formal practice. One may also just end up lifting heavy boxes or whatever in the course of one's life, which is life practice. This distinction comes from meditation (I am specifically getting it from Shinzen Young), where in formal meditation practice, one sits in silence and meditates (which is what people normally imagine when they hear the word "meditation"), whereas in life meditation practice, one tries to apply the insights from formal practice in everyday situations or try to achieve meditative states while doing daily tasks. [12] In therapy, one has actual, scheduled sessions with the therapist, but one might also have "homework" (stereotypically, the therapist writes down a statement on an index card that you then carry with you for the week, as you test out a new belief or self-image or whatever). Here is another difference with brain retraining, where at least in the way I practice it, basically the entirety of brain retraining is life practice. In brain retraining, you learn the concepts and techniques, but after you know what you are doing, there is basically no equivalent of "formal sitting practice" or "therapy session". It's all just integration practices: you just try to do the daily tasks of living, and symptoms and thoughts will come up, and you just deal with them using what you have learned; that is the whole of the work. Some people like to schedule in explicit times to do e.g. somatic tracking practice or visualizations, and I know that some brain retraining programs like DNRS mandate formal practice (and even Gupta Program to a lesser extent), but I have rarely done this.

So, it's not really so much that the actual techniques one uses are different between meditation, therapy, and brain retraining – in all three cases, one might be doing some form of somatic tracking (focusing on a sensation with curiosity and kindness and non-resistance), or some flavor of noticing one's thoughts and not believing or getting sucked into them, or relaxing the body, or feeling one's emotions (of course, each modality will emphasize or de-emphasize certain ways of doing each of these techniques). Instead I see the difference here as how much life practice is emphasized.

Another important difference that I already discussed above in the "Branching out" section is the distinction between "mindset" and "structure". Meditation and therapy only deal with the "mindset". But I also needed "structure": actual physical/cognitive schedules/rules of how much to push and when to push vs pull back. Miguel's progress cycles model says when to increase or decrease activity. Meditation says nothing about this topic, even if it says very helpful stuff about what to do when you encounter stuff that happens in meditation, like kriyas (involuntary movements that sometimes happen to meditators) or visual hallucinations.

Finally, there's something to be said about curation and exposition, as well. Finding the meditation or therapy practices that most help with physical symptoms takes a lot of experimentation. Therapy practices like IFS or coherence therapy that focus on healing the "root cause" (e.g. childhood trauma) will only help if that kind of trauma is driving the feeling of danger (John Sarno, who is a pioneer in the mindbody world, emphasized this kind of trauma as the root cause of chronic pain; but later mindbody teachers like Dan Buglio go against this, saying that trauma is only one way that the brain can create danger). And I think insight practice/vipassana is probably a bad idea for people going through severe illness, and concentration practice might not be possible. Also, excluding the aspects of Buddhism that are most confusing and counterproductive to healing seems helpful. The last thing someone with severe symptoms wants to hear are terms like "links of dependent origination" or be handed a Rob Burbea book. I think the Gupta Program does a good job of presenting Buddhist-inspired stuff without the historical/spiritual parts of it, so that even people who are really ill can just get going and actually do the work.

Legitimate scams, and the poor marketing of brain retraining

One of the phrases that keeps coming up in my head is "legitimate scams". Does the Gupta Program convey life-changing information? In my opinion, yes, it does. But does it need to charge $500 for a one year subscription that essentially consists of pre-recorded videos that one can watch? No, it should cost way less than this to provide this service and still be profitable enough to be doing. As far as I understand, the Gupta Program is one of the cheaper programs, too.

So are the critics right, in that brain retraining programs are overpriced and exploitative of desperate, ill people? In a sense, they are! [13] But the programs also provide amazingly useful information to people like me.

Part of the problem is that I think the high cost and secrecy of these programs creates an incentive to actually stick to the program. The actual ideas are so simple, and sound so close to ideas like CBT, that I think most people would immediately round off the actual ideas to the nearby ideas they are familiar with, and dismiss these programs as frauds. In other words, I suspect there is an inoculation/"rounding off" effect happening, where brain retraining sounds a bit too much like the extremely wrong things doctors have sometimes told patients (such as Graded Exercise Therapy, which is basically "keep gradually increasing your activity levels without paying any attention to your mental state or responding well to symptoms", which is a recipe for disaster), so people who have been sick for a very long time are unable to properly "hear" what brain retraining even is.

I don't really have a solution to this problem, but I am hoping this blog post can become part of one. I think one thing that has been sorely missing in the brain retraining space is a no-nonsense, no-woo, just plain simple state-it-like-it-is explanation of brain retraining and how it is supposed to work, so this is what I attempted above.

Ironically, despite seeming so "scammy" and "salesy", brain retraining has in my opinion a marketing problem. There are not enough people trying to explain it in simple, skeptic-friendly terms. All communication with the "outside world" (i.e. the world outside of brain retraining communities) seems to consist of marketing and "success stories" that almost never go into any detail about the epistemic aspects. There is no dialogue.

I find it tragic that so many people with a chronic illness are so quick to dismiss brain retraining. This is especially ironic since people with complex illnesses often have their experiences repeatedly invalidated by the medical establishment (e.g. being told that "your symptoms are all in your head", as was implied to me by several doctors). Yet they are the ones who are most vocal in invalidating people's experiences with brain retraining.

How I almost figured out mindbody stuff several times in the past, and why I gave up on it each time

Looking back at my own information consumption, I can see now that there were several times when I almost figured out the mindbody stuff, but each time I didn't have a breakthrough/recovery. I think it is interesting to discuss these, although I don't have any neat conclusions to draw.

Here are the instances of me encountering mindbody stuff that I can recall:

  • I've known about John Sarno since probably 2015 or so (and I've seen Sarno's name mentioned numerous times in various places in rationalist spaces).
  • I remember reading SSC's book review of Howard Schubiner's book a very long time ago, probably when it was published in 2016.
  • I had read Steve Byrnes's post about his RSI when it came out and had also read his earlier page about his RSI in maybe 2018–2019 (I vaguely recall that Steve had linked to it in some comment thread on probably Facebook).
  • I also read a book called the DP Manual back in 2019 or 2020, which is about how to recover from depersonalization (which at the time I thought was perhaps my root problem). The DP Manual says some stuff that vaguely sounds like mindbody stuff, including talking about the DP symptoms as a bully.
  • In 2021, Vipul Naik advised me to try EFT tapping. (This was the video I used.) It basically involves feeling into symptoms and saying some affirmations while simultaneously tapping various parts of your body.
  • I have known about polyvagal theory/"window of tolerance" type stuff since maybe 2021; I remember one therapist I had telling me to try going out in the heat as exposure therapy and trying it a few times.
  • I read some chapters of Howard Schubiner's book in September 2023 when fellow rationalist-EA-etc-adjacent person Raj recommended it to me. After reading these chapters, I vaguely recall a period of about a week where I went around saying "I'm healthy!", seeing no change in my symptoms, and giving up.
  • I noticed that around February–April 2020, right when the COVID pandemic started to emotionally hit me, my symptoms got worse. In 2023, my mother (whom I live with) got COVID, and the morning after I found out, I woke up with tachycardia (which was unusual at the time for me), had trouble regulating body temperature, and had trouble standing up (which was quite unusual). It later became clear that I hadn't gotten COVID, i.e. that all of the symptoms were from the stress and worry. I think my view at the time was something like "Stress can exacerbate symptoms in this illness, just like it can make a lot of other things worse. In particular, it can sometimes cause short-term bursts of symptoms. But obviously the whole thing can't be just purely due to stress; that would be crazy. Yes, I should try to be calm, but being super calm isn't going to make all my symptoms disappear (evidenced by all the times I've felt totally calm but didn't magically have all my symptoms disappear). And besides, COVID is inherently stressful, what am I gonna do, not stress out about a dangerous virus when my life has already been ruined by one?"
  • I had known about DNRS and the Gupta Program since probably 2022 or 2023, and in early 2024 a friend got access to the Gupta Program and we clicked around watching some of the videos. I in particular remember the videos about the IFS part puppets, and making fun of those because they seemed so absurdly dumb.

I now recognize that all of these things are pointing at roughly the same thing, but also, in my view, they are all subtly wrong enough or misleading enough that it kept me from actually getting better through them. And it wasn't until I started going through the Gupta Program that mindbody stuff finally started to make sense to me. So what was misleading about these other resources?

I think Sarno and Schubiner are wrong in pinpointing childhood traumas as the root cause of pain. I think for most people with mindbody symptoms there isn't anything like that. Both Gupta and Steve Byrnes get this right by talking about a feedback loop that just exists on its own without needing anything external. Dan Buglio also keeps mentioning this in his videos, about how most people probably don't need to dig up past traumas to heal.

Steve Byrnes and the comments on his post are misleading in that they give the impression that if it works, it will work very quickly. Gupta again is more accurate by saying it can take up to 6 months before you notice any improvements. Dan Buglio is more realistic, in saying that "book cures" are a small minority. Also, the other weird thing is that I think I was responding well to my symptoms most of the time. It just wasn't consistent, so if the symptoms got bad enough I would freak out. And this is what was probably maintaining the illness. Most sources don't talk about this aspect because they expect recovery to be very quick. Gupta/Dan/Miguel all emphasize consistency and repetition are what matter.

A lot of sources only focus on pain, whereas pain isn't really the main thing I've been dealing with. Gupta is right in saying it can cure basically anything, but this actually makes it more suspicious!

The sources I mentioned in my bulleted list also don't talk about pacing at all, possibly because they only talk about pain and they also expect success to be immediate. (Dan Buglio in my opinion also has this problem.) Whereas I believe pacing (or more specifically, what Miguel calls progress cycles) is very important both because the symptoms are real and because for severe cases like mine, trying to go fully back to normal activities will just backfire and make one's brain even more suspicious of this approach.

Gupta himself makes a few errors:

  1. He puts way too much emphasis on stuff like meditation and his 7 step technique. The techniques don't really matter; what matters is creating the feeling of safety. Listening to Dan and Miguel is what finally made me realize this.
  2. Pacing (as in, not overdoing activity) is important, but also pushing yourself a bit to create symptoms so that you can get practice dealing with symptoms is important. Gupta calls everything a "dip", whereas Miguel distinguishes between "adjustment periods" and "crashes". Adjustment periods are good and necessary for recovery. Gupta's view is more like "yeah, dips can happen, but that's okay, just keep doing the retraining", whereas Miguel is emphatic in saying "no, adjustment periods are the way you recover; you can't just lie down all day and expect to get better".

In the main place the DP manual talks about brain retraining-esque stuff, it calls the symptoms a "bully" and you should just avoid giving it attention, which is kind of right, but I think thinking of it as a bully is not the right analogy here. I really like Gupta's view of "the brain's priority is survival, and it thinks the symptoms are dangerous, so then it mobilizes more resources to fight the symptoms, which only creates more symptoms" as well as Miguel's "the body creates symptoms to slow you down, to prevent you from doing things, because doing things is dangerous" views much better. The key thing is that, unlike a bully, the brain isn't creating symptoms simply to torture you; it's creating the symptoms because it thinks the symptoms are somehow helpful, and so the recovery method has to reckon with this and somehow "convince" the brain that the symptoms are actually not needed anymore.

EFT is also similar. I think I was treating each EFT session individually, so that when I didn't see progress after trying it a few times I gave up on it. The information sources I had access to about EFT did not talk about this. But I can see how EFT could have worked now, if I had just kept doing it for like 6 months every time I got symptoms. I think EFT basically is a form of brain retraining. It's actually very similar to some parts of Gupta's 7 steps.

The polyvagal techniques I came across I also treated in a very one-off manner and when doing them a few times did not lead to any benefit, I gave up on them.

Generalizing from my own experience

If this could happen to me, could it happen to other people too? Brain retraining programs are full of recovery videos. I now think that almost all of these are legitimate. [14] Many people are recovering from bizarre symptoms, some even more intense than mine.

It seems clear to me that there are tons of people out there, suffering every day with symptoms, who are basically in the epistemic state I was in at the end of May 2024. Many of them probably even know about brain retraining, or other related terms like TMS, mindbody syndrome, psychophysiologic disorders, neuroplastic symptoms, and so on. But they don't think it could possibly work, or maybe they dabble with some techniques.

But I have no way of knowing what percentage of such people would actually be helped or cured by brain retraining. Do most people with, say, long COVID or MCAS or ME/CFS have a "truly physical" condition (not just physical symptoms, but the root cause is physical) such that brain retraining would do nothing for them, but there is some minority who are "mimics" that present with the exact same symptoms but have their brain/nervous system as the root cause? Could all or most such "complex chronic illness" cases be mindbody in nature, with a minority who have a physical root cause (due to e.g. organ damage from COVID infection or whatever)? Even more radically, could even some diseases with well-understood physical causes like autoimmune diseases or certain cancers or whatever also be helped by mindbody work? Could something totally insane like the Christian Science perspective that all illness is mental or spiritual have some truth to it?

Recovery stories give evidence about the wide variety of conditions for which people find mindbody work helpful, and also hint at the number of potential people it could help, but the selection effect (i.e. we never hear from the people who tried mindbody work for 6 months, saw no improvement, and moved on) makes it impossible to deduce any percentages of success.

I find all of this hard to think about, and I honestly have no idea what the truth is. I find myself sometimes becoming quite zealous about mindbody work, thinking thoughts like "Almost everything is mindbody!", and then feeling that writing a post like this one is the most important thing I could be doing, to help as many people experience the benefits I have experienced (this tends to happen when I emerge from an adjustment period and am feeling well). At other times, I find myself thinking that maybe mindbody work is a scam after all, heck, maybe it's not even going to work for me, what is the point of spending even more time on this post, is anyone even going to care about it? (this tends to happen when I'm deep in an adjustment period and symptoms I haven't had in months return).

I also want to mention that the poster child of ME/CFS, Whitney Dafoe, has in the last couple of years become able to eat solid foods and talk again, and his improvement curve and method seems extremely similar to brain retraining (although he seems to think it was maybe Joshua Leisk's Born Free Protocol that initially allowed him to start making the improvements).

I usually hate it when people cowardly say stuff like "well it's impossible to know, so I take an agnostic position" (e.g. about whether God exists). But sadly that is my current position when it comes to generalizing mindbody stuff to other people/diagnoses.

Luck-based medicine? and medical miracles

On the surface it seems like my experience of recovery is a confirmation of the luck-based medicine paradigm. I first tried both mainstream doctors and naturopaths; when both of those failed to help me, I started trying things without being too careful about having a solid model of why it would help me, instead relying on handwavy models or seeing what had worked for other people on internet forums or random-ish things that a health coach thought might work. I tried treatments that didn't work, and then the th one did work. But actually I disagree with luck-based medicine. I think luck-based medicine is fundamentally an anxiously oriented approach to recovery, this feeling of desperation, trying one thing after another. That might not be true for other people doing luck-based medicine, but it certainly was true for me when I was trying out all of the supplements and other treatments/palliatives earlier in my illness. What I had to do was to slow down, and fundamentally change my mindset. You could call this luck-based medicine on a higher level: I was luck-based medicining using one mindset, then popped back up the stack and went down another mindset. But again … I think this whole style of thinking is kind of misleading and not really helpful, in a way that I find hard to articulate.

On the topic of miracle cures, usually, miracle cures work only for a small number of people, which ought to temper my excitement about brain retraining. But there are two reasons I think the mindbody approach is at least somewhat of an exception.

First, it's not exactly a miracle. I've been at it for two years now, and still not at a level of health where I can hold down a job. Change is slow. I've taken away the feedback loops that have kept my illness going for so long. But recovery in this approach takes time, at least for me and many others (it can also be rapid for others, and so-called "book cures" are apparently a thing, although I think I've only heard of book cures in the context of chronic pain). In my mind, brain retraining is more like a skill, and it takes some people (like me) a very long time to acquire that skill. But, being a skill, I think pretty much everyone can learn it. Also, I think figuring out why some people recover so much faster than others is a very important topic to research, as it may help to devise programs to help people recover faster. Unfortunately the space seems resistant to such investigation, due to dynamics that I discussed in the "Legitimate scams" section. I think humanity is in the stone age when it comes to methods. [15]

Second, the approach's mechanism is so general, and has already worked for people with such varying conditions.

Being stuck in my head

One of the things that I have gradually realized, as I've gotten into mindbody work, is how much of my life I had spent being "stuck in my head". What I mean is that I had spent most of my life, probably starting around age 10–15:

  • Having conversations or arguments with people in my head
  • Feeling self-conscious whenever I was around other people, especially strangers
  • Prioritizing explicit reasoning above other kinds of knowing
  • Spending a lot of time on activities like math, programming, and analytic philosophy that prioritize explicit reasoning
  • More generally, spending most of my time thinking verbally or reading, being unable to and not wanting to switch off my brain in this way, a feeling that thinking a lot is virtuous (encountering LessWrong as a teenager further amplified this)

Others may describe this as being overanalytical, being addicted to thinking, etc.

This tendency interacted poorly with my chronic illness. In 2021, I started regularly logging symptoms that I was experiencing in a given moment or day using a checklist of symptoms on Google Forms. Then in 2022 I switched to logging symptoms in a more freestyle way on Roam, a note-taking app. My symptom logging became more extensive over time, until in 2024 when I was sometimes writing as much as 1,000 words on some days describing my symptoms. Logging my symptoms had turned into an obsession, but if someone had asked me at the time, I would have probably said something like "Well, maybe this is excessive or harmful, but I don't know what else to do! If I sit here and do nothing, I'm just wasting my life being ill. If I at least log my symptoms, I'm creating an artifact that can be analyzed, and maybe someone (or some AI) can spot patterns in my symptoms and figure out what I need to do to get better, or at least what my illness is called. Hey, maybe someone can work on a way to make it easier to analyze my symptoms!" You see, the pernicious thing about being stuck in my head was that it was self-reinforcing. There was a tinge of feeling virtuous, like this is what I am supposed to do, as a scientist/rationalist/thinker. The sicker I got, the more desperately I wanted to record everything and get better. When one is truly stuck in one's head, that feels like the right thing to do.

Being stuck in your head/stuck in your thoughts means when someone tries to help you by offering a different perspective, it just sounds like they are stupid, and you can always come up with clever and genuine-to-you seeming excuses not to take on such a perspective. The smarter you are, the more cogent your excuses will sound to you, and even to others. But, like Gary Drescher talks about in Good and Real, or the Escher painting mind, the problem is that you have multiple self-reinforcing beliefs such that it is not possible to change your mind in a piecemeal fashion. You must take in the mindbody perspective "all at once" in some sense, even if you hear bits and pieces and it builds in the background of your mind. That is why it is called the "mindshift" by Miguel Bautista: there is a distinct moment when the whole thing becomes felt in your whole being, when it feels so obvious and yet incommunicable to others.

Another aspect of being stuck in my head was the obsession with researching symptoms and my illness. I would spend hours on some days searching and reading posts on Reddit, and to a lesser extent Facebook groups and Twitter.

Being stuck in my thoughts wasn't really like dissociating from experience, in the way that one often hears about traumatized people. In fact, I was hyper-aware of my body and the symptoms I was experiencing. Instead, the distinguishing factor was that I was getting caught up in my reactions to my bodily experiences, looping on thoughts like "I have to log this symptom", "I need to figure out what this symptom is called and if anyone has a solution", "I hate this, make it stop", "Why is this happening to me and not other people? What did I do wrong?", and so on.

I can only see these patterns now that I am (to some extent) free of them.

I should however also mention that analytical thinking is still very much a good thing, in many situations. In fact, had I had a healthy nervous system and a different illness, perhaps obsessively logging symptoms and creating a medical hypotheses app really would have been the way to recover. This same obsessiveness is also to a large extent what is driving me to write this blog post, to explain it all in words, in the register of a typical LessWrong post, and I obviously think writing this post is a good use of my time. Some of these obsessive analytical tendencies may have also led me to eventually try brain retraining and to keep at it. So the moral is that analytical thinking can be very harmful, in particular when one's nervous system cannot handle the content of the thoughts themselves or the act of thinking precise thoughts. It can be tricky to figure out when one has crossed over from analytical thinking being useful to harmful, but I think the first step is to experience what not being in one's head is like at all, so that one can even consider such trade-offs.

Why did I become so ill? Understanding the deeper reasons for mindbody conditions

One of the things I learned as I watched many recovery stories on YouTube is that a lot of people have triggers for these conditions that aren't viral or bacterial. For example, Dan Buglio talks about how his back pain began one day when he went to put on his underwear. Miguel Bautista says he took too much pre-workout supplement (containing various stimulating substances). In both cases, the final trigger wasn't the real reason for the condition; it was something like a bunch of life stress piling up almost to the brink, such that a seemingly small thing pushed them over the edge.

Looking back at my own life, it started to make more sense that I had gotten this post-viral illness when so many others get viral illnesses all the time and go right back to full health after the acute illness. My family moved countries when I was a child, and I never fully adjusted to being in the US. I was extremely lonely and hated being in school. I had a pretty traumatizing romantic breakup as a teenager that I am pretty sure I still haven't fully recovered from. And of particular relevance to this audience, when I was a teenager I wandered onto LessWrong while looking for math textbooks and then found out about AI existential risk and slowly started to carry the weight of the whole world on my shoulders, while having no one I could talk to about any of this. [16] I believe that all of these events contributed to my stress level and created a sense that the world is not a safe place. And at the time I got the virus in 2019, I was stressed out about travel and also jet lagged. Even after I started to have this chronic illness, stressful things continued to pile on. In particular, in early 2020 I became incredibly stressed about the pandemic, and I noticed this led to an increase in symptoms.

Also looking back, I see that I already had some symptoms even before 2019. I remember in middle school I would have a period of about a month each year when I would have shortness of breath. I think I went to a doctor but I don't remember them doing anything about it, and it went away on its own. I also tended to be constipated despite eating a non-terrible diet, and this may have started as early as elementary school. I also remember going to the doctor once, maybe in high school, about feeling like there was an odd pressure in my gut. I sometimes had lower back and stomach pain as a teenager. In 2015 I almost fainted while showering once. None of these symptoms, other than the constipation (which eventually also led to a chronic fissure/hemorrhoids), were especially chronic; they would come and go. They also didn't limit my ability to be part of the world; they were annoying, mildly concerning, but also did not seem like a big deal.

I can now see clearly that all of these symptoms were early manifestations of mindbody symptoms. The symptoms were so different from each other, and occurred at different times, that it was not possible at the time to connect the dots. Like probably a lot things in life, these things only make sense in hindsight.

I mentioned near the beginning of the post that until 2022 I mainly believed that my symptoms were a result of anxiety. Given what I know now about how these mindbody conditions develop, does this vindicate my earlier point of view? To answer this question, it helps to think about what a diagnosis is even for. In my mind the purpose of a diagnosis is to quickly communicate a complicated condition by using a short label. This label can give information about the causes of the condition, which treatments may help, where to find a support network (e.g. patient forums), what needs a person might have, and so forth. The diagnosis "anxiety", at least to me, implies a bunch of things about the condition, including that it could be caused by a bunch of things like past traumas and stressful life situations (but not triggered by a viral illness), that treatments like therapy and medication are likely to help, that others who say they suffer from anxiety are similar to me in their capacity and needs, etc. I think such inferences someone would likely make based on the label "anxiety" are misleading. Yes, past traumas and stressful life situations did I believe contribute, but so did an intense viral infection. Treatments like therapy and medication did not help. And at least starting in summer 2024, my capacity and needs were vastly different from what one sees in anxiety sufferers.

Where I am now, and what is next?

I don't want to give people the impression that I have fully recovered. I still experience symptoms daily. As I write this, I am having a slight hunger attack because I've been writing all day and didn't do as good of a job consistently putting food in my mouth; and my thighs and knees are in some pain. But I have for the most part lost my fear of the symptoms. I struggle more with mental symptoms like depression and anhedonia, and "spiritual" symptoms like grief (of the time I have lost and continue to lose to this illness; the lives that have become impossible), loss of identity (I cannot have any identity at all, such as "person who is technical", because I know I can lose it all and have lost it all, but also, unlike having a Buddhist insight into no-self, this doesn't feel good at all), loss of purpose (I am healthy enough to chip away at writing posts like this and do some light programming, which is amazing compared to where I was a year ago, but I am still effectively disabled and wouldn't be able to hold down an actual job), alienation (almost no one understands what I went through, nor do they care, even though it was the single biggest and most confusing event of my life; what does that mean about relating to other humans, including the friends I had before I got sick?).

Currently I am probably as healthy as I was in 2021. I go on 25–40 minute walks most days, and have gone on 1 hour walks without too much issue, can get food from the kitchen without any issues, can sometimes even cook my own food, can read/watch videos/listen to music for hours without issue, can talk for hours with only slight feelings of being out of breath/tension, can sing, can ride the bus and leave the house as long as I've packed food, can be outside in 26 degrees Celsius weather and be okay, can shower standing and feel okay afterwards. I'm still somewhat limited in what I can eat. I still have brain fog and can't write or do technical things as well as I used to. I'm still more sensitive to the heat than normal people. I still can't work (I haven't tried, but I suspect I could only work maybe 1–4 hours a day sustainably with substantial difficulty). I can eat faster and I can easily go an hour without eating, but I still get hunger attacks if I push my limits. My lips were doing much better and looked normal except one spot that still peeled, but then this regressed for unknown reasons (now, as before the improvement, the whole lip peels endlessly like an onion until it starts bleeding, unless I put lanolin on every night after brushing my teeth). My swallowing problem has strangely not improved at all; I still take small bites and small sips, and often have to flap my hands to get the swallow reflex going.

I could still get COVID tomorrow and get long COVID. And then I would have to go through brain retraining all over again, which could take another 2 years. Or maybe it would be faster because I would already have built the skill. Or maybe brain retraining just wouldn't work at all, because I happen to get the variant of long COVID that is actually purely biological in nature and cannot be influenced by mindbody work. It's really hard to say what could happen.

I don't expect almost anyone who reads this to try brain retraining. Given the opportunity cost (i.e. it could take 3–6 months until any positive benefit is noticed, and that is assuming you do it consistently and "correctly"), probably it is not actually worth it for most people, unless they have a pretty severe chronic illness. I hope that better "techniques" can be devised such that people can reach insights and see improvements faster. If anyone reading this would like my help in doing brain retraining/mindbody work, I am willing (as my health and energy and time permit) to correspond via email at riceissa@gmail.com, or on a video call (email me to set something up). You can also leave comments on this post, but I don't check LessWrong very often so it may be a while before I reply. If you just want to get started without interacting with me, my playlist of YouTube videos is where I recommend starting.

item.title: Interpreting attention head outputs with NLAs
item.description:
Natural language autoencoders are pretty interesting; I'm a big fan of using meta-models to interpret what's going on inside LLMs and NLAs seem like a promising route to understanding them better.

One thing I've been interested in for a while is using NLAs to interpret the differences between activations: given an activation from an earlier and later layer, can we verbalize the changes between those two layers? It seems like it would be pretty cool if we could verbalize the activation diff between each layer in a transformer, since it would let us better understand how the model does computations.

Unfortunately training an activation-diff-NLA that actually works well is pretty hard[1], so I've done something easier: create an NLA that can interpret the outputs of the attention heads of a single layer (L24) of Qwen3-8B. It, uh, kinda works? I can get explanations that are (by the way the NLA is trained) text describing the attention head outputs! It's not clear to me how useful these explanations are though, and my NLA only works well for some attention heads.

Here's a widget where you can look at some example outputs from my NLA:

This is pretty early work, and I'll probably make better versions of this kind of thing in the future! I'm not really sure how good head NLAs are because I'm not sure how to evaluate them well. Please keep in mind that I've probably made some mistakes here, and you should generally take any results here with a grain of salt.

NLA recap

[You can skip this section if you're already familiar with NLAs.]

A traditional natural language autoencoder (NLA) is two models that are fine-tuned from the model we want to interpret: an activation verbalizer (AV) that takes in an activation at a specific layer as input and outputs text, and an activation reconstructor (AR) that takes that explanation as input and outputs an activation (specifically the AR is truncated at the layer the activation is from[2]).

First the AV and AR are SFTed on a bunch of Claude-written explanations on random tokens from random documents, that are written by giving Claude some context and asking it to make up something that seems like the model could plausibly be thinking about. Then the AV and AR are trained together to try to make it so when you take an activation h (from a random token from a random document), [3] (where ), with a KL penalty to keep the AV from straying too far from the SFTed AV. The AV is RLed with GRPO, and AR is directly optimized.

Matryoshka NLAs are my variant of NLAs where you randomly truncate the explanations during training, to try to make the most important information be at the beginning.

defining attention head NLAs

Qwen3 concatenates the per-head outputs (attn_weights @ v) of each attention head into one big vector, then multiplies that by the output matrix. Effectively the output matrix is projecting each attention head's output from a d_head-vector to a d_model-vector and summing over all the heads. But we can also use it to project just a single head into d_model-space and use that to interpret the output of a single attention head (Qwen3 doesn't have a bias for the output projection).

An attention head NLA is like a normal NLA, but instead of being given a normalized activation, it's given the normalized output of a single attention head (specifically, what you would get if you zeroed out all the other attention heads when doing output projection). Also, the AR is told what attention head it's looking at in its prompt, to try to make it so the AV doesn't start by encoding that information using some code to get cheap FVE (fraction of variance explained).[4]

Actually, instead of using just the attention head outputs, I took a bunch of attention head outputs over many tokens to get the average output, and subtracted the head's mean projected output from the attention head outputs. (I calculated the mean value once and reused it for everything.) In hindsight I think this was bad and I shouldn't have centered the outputs like that.

grouped query attention

Qwen3 models use grouped query attention (GQA) to make inference faster - specifically, the key and value matrices are tied for the 4 attention heads in each GQA group. The query matrices aren't tied, so the attention patterns among attention heads in a GQA group will differ: each head has its own query but shares the keys that the query looks for.

I didn't investigate the impact of GQA on my NLAs too much. It seems that often if my head NLA is good at explaining one head in a group it's roughly as good as the other heads in the group; I don't know why this is.

the explanations

Mostly when I look at explanations from my attention head NLA, I think "Yeah, that seems like something vaguely like what the attention head might be doing". I don't have much evidence on how useful this NLA is for understanding what attention heads do; I hope to have more information about that in the future.

evaluating them

It's pretty hard to evaluate attention head NLAs well, since we don't really have a good ground truth for what individual attention heads do. I'm pretty unsure what exactly is going on in the AV that makes it write the explanations the way it does (aside from the warmstart pushing it to write in a certain format initially). Often the explanations don't seem to be very relevant to the input text (despite having high FVE). I don't think this is that surprising - probably the model really is thinking about that thing for some reason, and it just ultimately doesn't end up being useful. I slightly prefer looking at the matryoshka NLA explanations since they can frontload the important stuff into the first several tokens and so I don't need to read the whole thing.

It would be interesting to try seeing the impact of ablating attention heads, and seeing if you can predict that impact from attention-head-NLA explanations.

quoting

The head NLA will often quote tokens that the attention head attended to. The head NLA doesn't get to directly see what tokens the attention head attended to (just the centered attention head output), so this is some weak evidence that the head NLA is actually doing something meaningful.

is it a hidden code?

I did some cursory analysis to see if the NLA was writing in some kind of hidden code, instead of just plainly describing the head's write. Having Claude Haiku 5.5 rewrite explanations (on held-out chat samples) to keep the substance but change the wording resulted in only losing 3.9 points of FVE (2.7 points for the matryoshka one). So it's probably not the case that the AV is writing in some shared code language for the AR.

how I trained these NLAs

I started with an SFT warm-start with explanations written by Claude Haiku 5.5, given a list of tokens that the attention head boosted, for each attention head, for 100k tokens (10 tokens from 10k FineFineWeb documents) when the centered attention head write was injected into the model as a soft token. This was a kinda arbitrary way of doing it but it didn't need to be great; I just needed a starting point for the NLA that pointed it in the right direction.

These explanations weren't intended to be very good, but they were enough to give the NLA a starting point that wasn't awful and made it so the explanations were written in a vaguely sensible way. I did ~0.35 H100 hours of SFTing on Qwen3-8B. I do everything on all attention heads of layer 24 (with one NLA shared across all heads), and train everything as unquantized (bf16) LoRAs.

After that I did 400 RL steps (with the same mechanism as for normal NLAs (based on the EasyNLA self-contained config[5])) for 8 H100 hours.

Once I had the normally trained NLA, I tried doing some extra training on top of it to convert it into a matryoshka NLA. I mostly did this because I wanted to make it easier to understand the explanations I was getting from the NLA, since I wasn't sure how much of the explanation text was actually relevant (versus filler text that wasn't actually used by the AR).

I did 240 steps with the matryoshka objective (truncating the explanations to U[1,120] tokens) on top of the normal-head-objective NLA to make the matryoshka head NLA variant for 2.7 H100 hours.[6] For the first 40 steps I only trained the AR so it learned to handle truncated explanations first. The switch to the matryoshka objective caused the FVE to drop initially because the AR wasn't expecting truncated explanations, but it caught up quickly.

Here's the FVE on held-out data, for both the standard and matryoshka NLAs (x-axis is log(step)):

Here's the train-time FVE for the standard NLA; if you plot it against training steps on a log plot the FVE grows with log(steps):

The KL penalty turned out to have been too low; the explanations drifted pretty far from the warm-start.

(Note that the way FVE is computed for NLAs is a little weird, and not what I expected at first. Mostly this is because the AR can't guess the mean vector, because the mean vector isn't unit length.)

reconstruction quality

The head NLA is better at some heads than others, and roughly tends to be about as good among heads in a GQA group:

It might be that the NLA kinda learns to specialize more in heads that are easier to verbalize.

misc graphs

These ones aren't that interesting but I had Claude make some other graphs in case you wanted to see them.

On the matryoshka NLA here's the FVE when truncating to various token counts on held-out pretraining documents:

Here's a better way to see how similar the FVE is among heads in the 8 GQA KV groups:

Here's how much more quoted tokens are attended to:


attention sinks

Qwen3 doesn't have an explicit beginning-of-sequence token, so instead attention heads rest unused attention on the first token. For the chat-tuned model this isn't really a problem though because the first token is always <|im_start|>, although the NLA was trained on web text which wasn't chat-formatted. I did some quick checks and it doesn't seem like attention sinks contribute to the FVE of my NLA much.

what should I think of activation diffs as

I kinda think of the activations after a layer in the residual stream as the "mental state" of an LLM at that point, and so I guess attention head outputs should be thought of as a change to that "mental state".

I'm not sure if this is the best way to think of the attention head output vectors though. For example, it might be that a model splits something I would think of as one logical change across multiple layers, and so there might not be a good explanation for what a single attention head (or layer) does - you might need to think about things more holistically, which is harder.

future directions

Ways you could improve head NLAs

  • It's kinda weird for the model to go from having normal activations in the residual stream to having diffs there. There's almost certainly a better way to give the attention head output vectors to the model.
  • Improve the way attention head outputs are centered (or maybe just don't center them?)
  • Comparing them to other ways of interpreting what attention heads do
  • Probably you could twiddle the hyperparameters (e.g. learning rate) to make it better
  • Try training one for a model that doesn't use GQA, so each attention head is more individually meaningful
  • Increase the KL penalty so that it's large enough to meaningfully affect training
  • Train it for more steps, use a bigger model, do full-parameter fine-tuning instead of a LoRA, etc.
  • Looking at a bunch of explanations and trying to understand them deeply
  • Have some explicit handling for attention sinks
  • Reward it for being good at all attention heads, instead of just effectively averaging the reconstruction error across all attention heads
  • Train on the base model instead of the chat one

I think coming up with a better way to interpret changes in activations is more important than just making attention head NLAs better. IMO you should think of attention head NLAs as more of a stepping stone to an actually good mechanism for understanding individual changes to LLM activations.

Random other ideas:

  • Try giving attention patterns to a meta-model
  • Consider using a better way to score the NLA than just looking at the reconstruction error

conclusion

I'm pretty unsure if methods like NLAs will actually end up being useful for solving LLM interpretability, but it seems like they might be pretty useful! Understanding changes between activations seems pretty useful to me for figuring out what the heck LLMs are doing.

I'm trying to write about my research more frequently by giving more updates, and this post is a part of that. There's still a lot of stuff related to attention NLAs (e.g. evaluating them in an Actually Good way) to explore, and I'll be writing about what I'm doing more!

Thanks to Alibaba for helping advance the study of LLM interpretability by releasing Qwen3-8B! I'm also grateful for EasyNLA, which is a fork of nanoNLA, which in turn is a reimplementation of Anthropic's NLA code. I've published the source code I used and training run logs.

Please let me know if you have any advice/ideas for me; I'd love to hear what you think. :) Please experiment with new kinds of NLA yourself - there's a lot to discover here and it would be really great if we could solve interpretability!

This is the write-up of my MATS project so far, as a mentee of Abram Demski. Those who would prefer a more formal/academic/mathematical write-up should look at the AAMAS submission here.

TL:DR, a formal framework for representing CDT, EDT and UDT on the majority of classical Newcomblike problems, plus some accompanying results about how CDT can be made to pay for ignorance.

Introduction

I present my framework for hosting classical decision theories (Causal, Evidential and Updtateless/Functional decision theories) in classical Newcomblike problems. The framework is intended to be faithful (the outputs of the framework regarding what theories act in which ways in which problems agree with the consenus), fair (each theory's intuitions about "why this is rational behaviour" can be expressed as formal properties of the framework, the framework tries to avoid "begging the question" in favour or against any particular theory) and computable (given a formal description of any theory and any problem (at least those that the framework can express) there is a simple algorithm do determine what that theory would do in that problem. To the best of my knowledge, there is no other framework that fulfills these three properties while hosting CDT, EDT and UDT.

We can broadly divide Newcomblike problems into two categories: read problems (the world varies with the agent by reading the agent, e.g Newcomb's Problem) and write problems (the world varies with the agent by writing some portion of the agent, e.g Smoking Lesion). My framework only handles read problems, rejecting write problems mostly as a consequence of giving agents perfect introspection.

The most significant finding from my framework thus far is that a calibrated[1] CDT agent will in some cases pay to receive reduced information, and objectively benefit for doing so. To the best of my knowledge this is an orginal result.

This choice avoids phenomena such as an agent's action at a particular observation rendering that observation logically inconsistent with the agent (and thus making the choice of action difficult to analyse) or an agent making a certain observation and concluding with logical certainty how they are about to act. For maximum flexibility I allow this, though I do also formalise why we might want to say that some such comparisons are illegitimate (mostly if the two theories reach those branches at very different rates).

Agent Beliefs

Agents believe that the problem functions exactly as described by . They are not required to hold any beliefs about the explicit probability of themselves performing certain actions. 

Note that the agent only has access to the predictor through its description in , which gives only the parameters of the predictor (accuracy, predicted observation, response to prediction) and describes nothing of how the predictor works or what it will actually predict. The predictor, on the other hand, has direct access to the decision policy of the agent and its output on . This prevents circular dependency or the agent trying to "game" the predictor. It also preserves the decision-sensitivity of the predictor.

Epistemologies

Since agents do not (necessarily) have any beliefs about the action they will take, nor any beliefs about what exact action will be predicted, the agent cannot straightforwardly evaluate the probability of being in any particular start state or the expected utility of the various accessible actions. An epistemology is the device that fixes this gap. Different epistemologies emit different data shapes as required for different decision procedures.

Prediction-Skeptic Epistemology

Prediction-Skeptic epistemology refuses to accept and/or make use of the decision-sensitivity of the predictor. In particular, Prediction-Skeptic epistemology holds that it is appropriate to determine about your beliefs regarding what the prediction is likely to be, and then to reason about what action you should take without ever updating your beliefs about the prediction.

The crucial and quintessential property of updateless decision theories is that the initial choice of policy is made without consulting the observation, selecting whatever policy does best overall. This leads to the property that UDT is unbeatable (in expectation) on any decision space , and also to the property that a UDT agent will sometimes voluntarily sacrifice utility for a benefit that that instantiation of the agent will never see.

Evaluation

We evaluate decision theories on Decision Problems rather than only on Decision Spaces. This is a strictly broader notion as, in this framework, a Decision Problem can be any subset of the observation space of a Decision Space, including the entire Decision Space. The main reason for this choice is the desire to create a framework that, as far as possible, is "fair" to all decision theories in that it allows their favoured arguments and counter-arguments to exist as formal properties of the framework, and tries not to rule those arguments invalid by definition.

Permitting evaluation only at the level of Decision Spaces would provide a clear argument in favour of UDT, as (provably) UDT can never be beaten at this level, and strictly beats every other formalised theory in at least one well-known problem. However, this argument would be won by side-stepping, rather than directly addressing, the updateful argument that UDTs willingness to voluntarily burn to death is a meaningful downside.

The framework does also contain the means to argue that bomb-branch style comparisons are unfair in some way, by the notion of "comparison-calibration".

Calibration

I define three notions of calibration. The first two relate to agents within decision spaces/problems, and the third compares two agents within a decision problem.

Observation-Calibration

A decision procedure is observation-calibrated on some decision problem  if its beliefs about what state it is likely to be in (conditional on the observation) are correct.

Generative-Calibration

A decision procedure is generative-calibrated at  if its beliefs regarding how likely it is to be in any particular state (not conditioning on the observation) are correct. In other words "how likely is an agent like me to find themselves in any particular state if they were to play this game from scratch?"

The Fully Transparent and Updateless epistemologies are observation- and generative-calibrated everywhere all the time (Updateless epistemology is always observation-calibrated even though it arguably doesn't care about being so). Partially transparent is always observation- and generative-calibrated at  (the predicted observation) and mostly not calibrated otherwise[5]. Prediction-Skeptic epistemology is mostly not calibrated[5].

Comparison-Calibration

Comparison-calibration is measured on a set of Decision Procedures (typically 2) relative to a Decision Problem  in Decision Space  and it measures the ratio of how frequently each Decision Procedure encounters that specific Problem in  (or the ratio of the most and least frequent if comparing more than 2 Procedures).

Worked Examples

Newcomb's Problem

I tweak some of the numbers here to make the mathematics a little simpler, but this is scructurally Newcomb's Problem.

You find yourself in a room with two boxes, one small transparent box and one large opaque box. By some reliable method you learn the following facts:

  • The large box contains either $1 or $10.
  • The big box is completely opaque, soundproof etc. there is no way to work out how much money is in the big box without opening it.
  • By some fancy mechanical system, you must either open only the big box (1Box) or both boxes (2Box).

Even against people who try all manner of psychological tricks or last-minute changes-of-mind, the predictor is 99% accurate.
  • Nonetheless, the amount of money in the large box was fixed a week ago, shortly after the prediction was made. There is no hidden trapdoor in the big box, and no temporal wormhole for the predictor to peek through.
  • The process by which people are invited to play this game is uniformly random, so the kind of agent you are/the decision you would make has no bearing on how likely you are to encounter this problem in the first place.

Prediction-Skeptic CDT straightforwardly concludes that it will get an extra dollar by two-boxing, and two-boxes. Note that since two-boxing causally dominates one-boxing for this problem, the exact prior beliefs about the prediction do not matter, as long as they are held independent of the agent's action.

Verdicts - NR-CDT

The argument here goes something like "One-boxing is irrational because if I know I am about to one-box, my beliefs about the likely state of the world will tell me that two-boxing would be better, making it irrational to actually follow through and one-box. On the other hand, if I know I am about to two-box, I should still two-box, therefore two-boxing is rationally defensible".

Verdicts - EDT

"If I know I am about to one-box, then I expect to receive far more money than if I know I am about to two-box, therefore one-boxing is much better news than two-boxing, therefore I should one-box."

Verdicts - UDT

"The overall best-performing agents are one-boxers, therefore I should be a one-boxer."

Transparent Newcomb is extremely similar to Newcomb's problem, the main difference being that the large box is also transparent, clearly displaying how much money it contains. This also leads to the secondary change that the predictor only cares about what you would do if you saw $10 in the big box (this is to prevent "impossible-to-predict" agents who would always do the opposite of the revealed prediction).

Optimality Conditions

This formalises the idea that "UDT cares about decision spaces, EDT cares about observations and CDT cares about states".

Equivalence Conditions

Various decision theories recommend the same action on some problems. For example, it is generally accepted that EDT and UDT agree on Newcomb's problem (both one-box) and that EDT and CDT agree on Transparent Newcomb (both two-box). I can prove some general rules about when various decision theories agree. I only claim that these results hold in the simplified world of my framework, not necessarily in all conceivable Newcomblike problems.

Singleton Observation  UDT = EDT

If  contains only a single starting observation (meaning ), then UDT and EDT endorse exactly the same set of policies up to tie-breaking. This is because a single starting observation in some sense forces EDT to be updateless, because the agent gains no information about where they are in the problem before making the observation, therefore the optimal policy before making the observation (UDT) is the optimal policy conditional on making the observation (EDT).

Note that this result alone shows that the (tickle-free) Smoking Lesion cannot be faithfully represented in this framework (at least according to the view that EDT refrains from smoking in tickle-free Smoking Lesion while UDT smokes). This is because if the agent perceives the world in exactly the same way regardless of being affected by the lesion or not (i.e one starting observation) then EDT and UDT must recommend  the same action. I argue in "Write Problems" that this is at least partly because Smoking Lesion is not clearly well-formed for perfectly introspective agents.

Singleton Predicted Observation   EDT = CDT

If the predicted observation o' is fully observable (meaning ) then EDT and CDT (under the same transparency variant) endorse exactly the same set of policies up to tie-breaking, and PS-CDT agrees with both at . This is because observing  provides 100% certainty about which state the agent is in, meaning that, conditioning on observing , the chosen action informs expected utility only through  and  (the predictor has no influence after conditioning on  as  is now known) which both EDT and CDT respect equally.

Given that they act the same at , EDT and CDT (with matched transparency) will also act the same at all other observations, since either their beliefs about the prediction agree (fully transparent) or they both assume the prediction is uniform random (partially transparent).

Not Decision-Sensitive  UDT = EDT = CDT

If  is not decision-sensitive (every possible policy sees the same distribution over start states). Then UDT, EDT and CDT all endorse the exact same policies. This is because all three theories are happy to fix their beliefs about the probabilities of states before reasoning about how to act, and all agree exactly on the probability distribution over states. Therefore acting to maximise expected utility treating the state, observation or decision space as fix all produce the same results.

This result should not be read as "decision-sensitive predictors are the only phenomemon where UDT, EDT and CDT disagree" but "decision-sensitive predictors are the only phenomenon formalisable in thsi framework" where the three disagree.

Write Problems

To my understanding, the key and defining feature of Newcomblike problems is that they force some significant feature of the problem to be statistically correlated with the eventual decision of the agent (in at least one branch of the problem) despite said feature being causally prior to the agent's decision. This can be done by having the agent's eventual decision influence the initial state of the problem (typically through decision-sensitive predictors) (read problems) or by having the initial state of the world influence the agent's eventual decision (write problems).

To be properly Newcomblike, the influence in write problems should in some way sidestep the normal operation of the agent's Decision Procedure, otherwise every decision problem where the agent learns something would technically be a Newcomblike problem, since the starting observation in the problem does influence the agent's final action.

Unfortunately I cannot represent write problems in my framework, though I think that the reasons why are themselves instructive. To illustrate them, I will use the example of Smoking Lesion.

Smoking Lesion

The problem of Smoking Lesion can be described roughly as follows:

  • In a parrallel universe, smoking has no negative (causal) impacts on a person's health.
  • However, there is still a strong correlation between smoking and getting cancer. This is because of a particular genetic condition (the "smoking lesion") that causes people to be predisposed towards both smoking and cancer.
  • You are an inhabitant of this universe deciding whether you should smoke.
  • You would like to smoke, you don't want cancer, and you would prefer not smoking without cancer to smoking and having cancer.

The classical consensus on this problem is that CDT and UDT smoke freely, and that EDT refuses to smoke because of the correlation between smoking and cancer.

The Tickle Defence

If we assume that the smoking lesion works by producing a strong desire to smoke, or by making smoking more appealing or enjoyable, then we can argue that EDT also smokes freely. This is because upon observing within itself the desire to smoke, the EDT agent then learns everything it could learn about how likely it is to have the lesion, meaning that its eventual decision to smoke or not will carry no further information about how likely the agent is to have the lesion, meaning that the agent can smoke freely.

Tickle-Free Smoking Lesion

If we want the classical Smoking Lesion verdicts (where UDT and CDT smoke and EDT doesn't) we could imagine that the lesion works in some other way, that does not alert the agent (so that EDT treats the decision to smoke as evidence of the lesion). For example, perhaps the lesion induces some completely invisible (to the agent), subconscious bias towards smoking.

However, if the lesion and its effects are entirely invisible to the agent, this would mean that UDT and EDT must agree on the verdict (see the results above), meaning my framework cannot host the tickle-free smoking lesion with its classical verdicts. This is unsurprising as I have no mechanic that could simulate a subconscious bias, but it is also not clear how such a bias would work.

I couldn't model the lesion's effect by biasing the agent towards a certain decision theory, since an agent could then get evidence on whether it has the lesion by considering what kind of decision theory it has. Furthermore, I want the framework to be "theory-neutral" to the extent that I can drop in any kind of agent and meaningfully compare them on the "same" problem[7].

I couldn't model the lesion's effect by having some probability of forcing the agent's final output, since then the output of the EDT algorithm carries no information about whether the agent has the lesion, only whether or not that output is ignored does.

I think that the statement of Tickle-free Smoking Lesion is at least partially incoherent. We state "there is a statistical correlation between choosing to smoke and having the lesion" and then ask "what would UDT/EDT/CDT do?" This question seems to imply a deterministic answer to each of these questions, which is only compatible with the correlation if we assume that EDT agents never have the lesion. But then knowing oneself to be a follower of EDT would be extremely strong evidence against having the lesion, as outlined above.

That said, it does appear that invisible (or near-invisible) subcoscious biases can exist in humans, which suggests that Tickle-free Smoking Lesion is coherent at least for human-like agents. I think the main reason for this is that humans are not perfectly introspective agents. Any agent with perfect introspection[8] should be able to identify the presence or absence of whatever means the lesion uses to influence the final decision, meaning that an EDT version of such an agent will never gain additional information from observing its final decision and can freely smoke.

Therefore the only ways to make this work as far as I can see would be to remove perfect introspection from the agents, or to allow the agents to have very strong (possibly Knightian) uncertainty about how the correlation in Smoking Lesion actually works. Either of these would require interesting but non-trivial adaptations to the model. 

Value-of-Information

EDT Will Pay for Ignorance

A well-known criticism of EDT (especially from academic Causal Decision Theorists) is that EDT is inherently irrational because it acts more in the manner of "managing the news" than actually trying to get good things to happen.

One of the most damning (at least according to EDT's critics) examples of this is EDT's willingness to pay considerable amounts of utility to not be told free information in certain Newcomblike problems.

For example, suppose that an EDT agent is about to enter a room where a game of Transparent Newcomb has been set up (the prediction has already been made). Suppose that someone outside the room offers the agent a blindfold, preventing them from seeing how much money is in the big box. If the blindfold is "visible to the predictor"[9] then wearing it essentially turns the game into Newcomb's problem. If we use the formalisations above, a fully-calibrated EDT expects to gain $9.90 from Newcomb's problem but only $1.10 from Transparent Newcomb (correctly for both problems). Since choosing to wear the blindfold would influence the EDT agent's beliefs about how it would act in the room and hence how much money is ultimately likely to be in the box, it appears that an EDT agent would not only wear the blindfold but would pay up to $ for the privelege.

While they disagree on how you should actually act in Newcomb's problem and Transparent Newcomb, both UDT and CDT agree that the two problems are largely equivalent and that you should mostly perform the same action in both problems[10]. In fact, UDT would pay a very small amount of utility to refuse the blindfold so that it can freely two-box if it sees the large box empty (which happens 1% of the time). There seems a fairly wide consensus that "pay $ for reduced information" is an accurate description of what EDT would do, but it is shared mostly amongst Causal and Updateless decision theorists. I am not aware of an authoritative EDT treatment of this formulation of the problem.

The Merge Operator

We can formalise this notion of "putting on the blindfold" in my framework. Whenever we have a decision space  with some non-predicted observation  such that  we can propose the new decision space  where and . Note that only the observability of the problem is affected, everything else stays the same.

For example, applying this operator to the formalisation of Transparent Newcomb above yields exactly the formalisation of Newcomb's problem.

CDT Will Pay for Ignorance

While it is often accepted that paying for ignorance is a behaviour unique to EDT, it can be shown that in some problems, CDT also exhibits this behaviour.

Mechanical Newcomb

Mechanical Newcomb can also be described as "Causal Newcomb's Problem".

  • Both boxes are made of a wire mesh and hence mostly transparent. The boxes are far enough apart that you can only reach one at a time.
  • The large box contains $10 and the small box $1.
  • Opening the large box permanently locks the small box, meaning that two-boxers must start with the small box.
  • Opening the small box triggers the flamethrower to incinerate the contents of the large box.

Since this problem does not involve any kind of decision-sensitive prediction, all of CDT, EDT and UDT agree (that you should one-box).

Mechanical Newcomb by itself is (I think) largely uninteresting, but it can be used to build interesting problems.

If heads, the room is set up according to Newcomb's Problem and the prediction. If tails, the room is set up according to Mechanical Newcomb (no prediction needed).

Semi-Mechanical Newcomb (Opaque)

The same problem, but with the lights turned off, meaning the agent can no longer see which sub-game they are playing.
